pages.text: Jersey gas bills to rise as Middle East turmoil persists Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Gas bills to rise as Middle East turmoil persists 6 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jonathan Morris Channel Islands Press Association Island Energy said customers can contact its customer team for support Gas customers in Jersey will see their bills increase by about 5% from 1 December after Island Energy announced a rise in tariffs for households and businesses. The company said its mains gas, mini bulk tank and cylinder tariffs would increase by 1p per kilowatt hour (kWh) for all domestic and commercial customers from 1 December 2026. It said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas and liquefied petroleum gas costs amid disruption to exports and shipping routes in the Middle East after the conflict with Iran. Chief executive Graeme Millar said: "We recognise that any price increase is unwelcome, particularly during winter." More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Securing fuel at lower prices in advance had limited the impact of wholesale cost increases on customers, Millar said. However, the energy boss added: "It cannot fully protect customers from sustained increases in the cost of fuel and bringing it to Jersey." They’re part of the sunflower family and, surprisingly, entirely unrelated to the globe artichoke. They produce tall, leggy stems upon which a bright yellow flower blooms, and while they lack the size and sturdiness of sunflowers, they make up for that by appearing in great numbers and developing edible tubers underground. Despite these admirable features, there are good reasons why they are not the most common sight. pages.text: Jess Carter: England defender joins Bay FC after leaving Gotham FC as free agent - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Jess Carter made 83 appearances across all competitions for Gotham FC Published 18 November 2026 England defender Jess Carter has completed a move to Bay FC after leaving Gotham FC as a free agent. The 29-year-old has signed a contract that will keep her with Bay FC - a club based in the San Francisco Bay Area - until 2028, with the option for an additional year. Carter joined New York-side Gotham in July 2024 after a six-year spell with Chelsea that saw her win the Women's Super League on five occasions. "Coming to Bay FC is a new challenge, and that's something I'm excited about," said Carter. "I've been fortunate to be part of some successful teams, and I know how much work goes into winning. I'm looking forward to getting to know this group, earning the trust of my team-mates and doing my part to help us move forward." Carter played in all 30 of Gotham's matches in 2026 as the club won the NWSL Shield - given to the league's regular-season champions. She also helped Gotham win the NWSL Championship in 2025, when they defeated Washington Spirit in the final. "Jess has been a big part of what we've accomplished as a club, and we're very thankful for the contributions she's made during her time here," said Yael Averbuch West, the president of football operations for Gotham. In this role, she provides executive leadership for the Federal Aviation Administration's efforts to safely integrate advanced aviation technologies into the National Airspace System (NAS), including uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS), electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, counter-UAS technologies, and other emerging entrants. She is responsible for developing enterprise-wide strategic and business plans, overseeing research and integration initiatives, coordinating with the Department of Transportation, other federal agencies, industry, and international stakeholders, and advancing policies that enable the safe expansion of advanced aviation technologies. Ms. Jones has more than 15 years of progressively responsible leadership experience in the Federal Aviation Administration, specializing in executive operations, strategic planning, national security, program management, and organizational governance. Jessica Kunkle Jessica Kunkle Jessica Kunkle is NNSA’s Associate Administrator for the Office of Infrastructure. She brings over 15 years of diverse experience, spanning infrastructure, nonproliferation, procurement, and budgeting. In her current role, Ms. Kunkle is charged with modernizing the Nuclear Security Enterprise to support the agency’s vital national security missions. Her passion for innovation, agility, and delivering results have enabled her to push the boundaries of NNSA’s real property acquisition strategy and accelerate infrastructure modernization via bold, proactive streamlining and non-traditional delivery approaches. She also led agency-wide improvement initiatives in the NNSA Program Executive Office and helped to secure vulnerable nuclear materials and radiological facilities around the world in the Office of Global Threat Reduction. pages.text: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono experiencing 'most difficult days of my life' - BBC Sport Figure caption, Fans pay respects to Tenerife's De Miguel By David Watkinson , BBC Sport senior journalist and Ffion Wynne , BBC Sport journalist Published 4 November 2026 FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel. Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday. The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week. Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally". "These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement. "I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened. "I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him. "I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing. "Rest in peace, Jesus." The Canary island is in mourning for the Tenerife striker, who died from injuries sustained in a collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a match on Monday. The 30-year-old had quickly established himself as a club favourite, scoring 11 goals in his first season as Tenerife were promoted to the second tier of Spanish football. But now the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez Stadium has become a shrine to the player, with hundreds of people gathering throughout the past few days to lay flowers, light candles and pay their respects. Bouquets, rosettes sent by clubs from across Spain, prayer cards, photographs, children's drawings and scarves have been laid around the grounds outside gate nine. It is a deeply moving scene. Fans and residents stand in silence, taking in the tributes. Many are visibly tearful as the scale of the loss begins to sink in at the very place the incident happened. pages.description: Goalkeeper Jesus Owono will miss Equatorial Guinea's Afcon 2027 qualifiers after asking to be left out of the squad following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
pages.text: Jesus de Miguel: Jesus Owono left out of Equatorial Guinea squad after death of Tenerife player - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Jesus Owono helped Equatorial Guinea to the quarter-finals of the 2021 Afcon but the National Thunder suffered a group-stage exit at the 2025 finals in Morocco Published 5 November 2026 Goalkeeper Jesus Owono will miss Equatorial Guinea's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers this month following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel. De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday. Owono said he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" in a statement issued by his club FC Andorra on Wednesday, adding that it is "very hard to come to terms with what has happened". Equatorial Guinea's football federation (Feguifut) said that the 25-year-old had requested to be left out of coach Vincenzo Alberto Annese's squad. Feguifut president Venancio Tomas Micha had previously said his organisation was offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player. Owono has been first-choice keeper for the National Thunder since November 2020 and has featured at the past three Afcons. Equatorial Guinea face Zimbabwe in a double-header in Group E, with a home match in Bata on Thursday, 12 November before a trip to Harare four days later. The two teams sit level on three points after two rounds of matches, with DR Congo top of the standings on six points and Sierra Leone pointless at the bottom of the table. I spent two years mapping the areas surrounding one of the most beautiful drives in the world. The Place The Icefields Parkway (Highway 93N), in Alberta, owes its name to the spectacular icefields and glaciers that line the road. The parkway, which is a 232 km stretch of highway cutting through Banff and Jasper National Parks, attracts between 1.2 million and 2 million visitors per year. From his introduction to folk dancing at a party in the summer of 1950 until he finally hung up his melodeon in 2015, folk and morris dancing were the mainstay of his life. He was a White Horse Morris dancer and musician, and dancer, musician and president of the Mendip Morris troupe. Mr. Lassek brings more than 30 years of oil and gas industry experience spanning resource development, engineering, operations, and technology development. He has held operator and service-company roles in the United States and internationally. His experience spans conventional and unconventional resources. Before joining DOE, he served as Global Senior Completions Advisor at Hess Corporation. He previously held senior technical roles with Newfield Exploration, Encana, and Ovintiv. He began his career at Schlumberger in domestic and international operations before moving into technology development and engineering leadership. When the authorities finally hauled it to the surface and towed it to Port Townsend, Washington, in June 2013, the Western Flyer looked like a ghost ship. Veils of seaweed hung from its rotting timbers, and it was encrusted with barnacles. The insides were full of mud. At the boatyard the wreck was valued at $0, but a purchaser from California, John Gregg, paid $1 million for it, or more precisely, for its mystique. pages.text: Join Open Jam Sessions for an Insight Into London's Grassroots Music Scene | National Geographic TRAVEL Join Open Jam Sessions for an Insight Into London's Grassroots Music Scene Across the city, a growing crop of music-making events is nourishing the capital’s grassroots music scene — and helping to alleviate loneliness in the process. The Five Points Jam brings together more than 30 musicians for high-energy performances. Richard Mukuze By Sam Kemp Published November 18, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The jazz saxophonist Stan Getz once said that the best music sounds “like a good conversation among friends”. Right now, some of the most interesting musical conversations in London are happening at its grassroots venues, where open jam sessions are giving musicians of all levels a platform to improvise, hone their craft and form new friendships. Participants may not know their fellow musicians, let alone the genre or dynamic, so there’s no choice but to embrace whatever the night brings. It’s about getting lost in music, together. London’s open jam scene really took hold in the years following the Covid lockdown — a period when music-lovers were looking for new ways to connect in a city beset by independent venue closures and the ongoing effects of social isolation. The Five Points Project, an events platform founded in 2022 by school friends James Lear and Max Riby-Williams, offered a solution: find a space, fill it with musicians and watch a community take shape. pages.text: Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand | National Geographic TRAVEL Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand A new off-grid tour takes travellers deep into New Zealand’s largest basin in search of the elusive black stilt. New Zealand's Southern Alps are home to one of the world's rarest birds: the black stilt. Natasha Bazika By Natasha Bazika Published June 11, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Clouds move quickly across the Mackenzie Basin, dragging shadows over braided riverbeds and dry tussock plains that stretch towards New Zealand’s Southern Alps. One moment, the landscape is washed silver; the next, it disappears beneath a sweep of weather rolling over the mountains. I’m heading deeper into this high country on a window of borrowed time, crossing the 46,950-acre wilderness of Glenmore Station, a merino sheep, deer and cattle station. Hours earlier, the same storm front had grounded my helicopter flight to the country’s highest whisky bar — The Bad Decision, on a saddle above Glenmore Station — before it could leave the tarmac. Now, I’m racing a temporary clearing in the weather to find something far more elusive than a dram of mountain liquor: the black stilt, or kakī in Māori, one of the rarest birds on the planet. “The Mackenzie Basin has its own weather system,” says guide Ben Laffan, who’s taking me on Tekapo Adventures’ Black Stilt birding tour , a newly launched birdwatching experience, directing our four-wheel drive up a rough track. Jonathan Brightbill Department of Energy General Counsel Jonathan Brightbill is General Counsel of the U.S. Department of Energy. He is a graduate of the Georgetown University Law Center and the University of Pennsylvania Wharton School of Business. Mr. Brightbill clerked for the Honorable D. Brooks Smith on the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. As General Counsel, Mr. Brightbill is responsible for overseeing the legal operations of the Department of Energy, as well as counseling the Secretary, Deputy Secretary and senior leadership on the execution of their duties in the development of federal energy policy. His oversight portfolio includes nuclear energy regulatory reforms, electricity and gas markets, energy efficiency, civilian nuclear programs, business transactions, international negotiations, loan and grant investments, and oversight of the Department’s national laboratory system. Prior to joining DOE, Mr. Brightbill was a partner in the Washington, D.C. office of Winston & Strawn. During the first Trump administration, he served as Acting Assistant Attorney General for the Environment & Natural Resources Division of the U.S. Department of Justice. pages.text: Josh Kerr: The Making of the Man Behind the Shades - BBC Sport By Richard Winton BBC Sport Scotland You know Josh Kerr, right? The guy with the shades. The fastest man to ever run a mile. Scottish, but with a curious transatlantic accent. Slicked-back hair. Beard. Usually got a medal of some kind slung around his neck. No stranger to telling you what he thinks. That's Kerr the competitor, one of the foremost faces in world athletics, and a man who rampaged around London's Olympic Stadium in three minutes 42.66 seconds in July to set a new world record - then followed it up with a home Commonwealth gold and an imperious triumph at the Ultimate Championship. Kerr recognises the description, smiling as it's articulated. But is there another version of him? Speaking to him during one of his regular returns to Scotland from his New Mexico base, it becomes clear there is. There's scant chat about records, medals and his enjoyably niggly rivalry with Jakob Ingebrigtsen. Instead, he talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, entering races under a false name, cold-calling universities, being starstruck meeting Scotland's rugby players and his granny keeping him humble. This is the Kerr who spent the thick end of an hour on a chilly August evening taking selfies, signing his name and sharing his wisdom with young fans at Scotstoun after his Commonwealth medal presentation. The Kerr who is still a regular visitor to first club Edinburgh AC's training sessions. This is Uncle Josh, who is heading for a party with his nephews after this chat. pages.text: Journey Into a Prehistoric Cave That Trapped and Entombed Animals for Millennia Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Photos courtesy of Dr. Susumu Tomiya and public domain Natural Trap Cave is a pit in northern Wyoming into which countless animals have fallen and met their untimely demise since the Pleistocene. Paleontologists today find the cave a treasure trove — a stunning record of the species that have long roamed the area. The mammalian fossils left behind shed light on the climate, food sources and migration patterns of these species from earlier eras. Careful excavation work over the years that has involved sifting for bones, extracting ancient DNA, and looking for prehistoric pollen has revealed not just the plants and animals that once populated this part of the world, but also the ecosystems and climates that governed it. It also has required some rather advanced rappelling skills. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with vertebrate paleontologist Julie Meachen and Smithsonian contributing writer Michael Ray Taylor about what rappelling into Natural Trap Cave reveals about its contents and what it can tell us about Earth’s past. Photo : Photo ONU / Manuel Elias Le 20 mars, l'ONU célèbre la Journée de la langue française Les Journées des langues aux Nations Unies ont été introduites en 2010 pour célébrer le multilinguisme et la diversité culturelle. L’ONU célèbre chaque année six « Journées de la langue », consacrées aux six langues officielles des Nations Unies, qui sont l’arabe, le chinois, l’anglais, le français, le russe et l’espagnol. Ces journées sont l'occasion de sensibiliser la communauté internationale à l'histoire, à la culture et à l'utilisation de chacune de ces langues. La date de la Journée de la langue française a été choisie symboliquement en référence au 20 mars 1970, qui marque la création de l'Agence de coopération culturelle et technique (ACCT), devenue l’ Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) . Le multilinguisme, plus fondamental que jamais Pour sortir de la crise provoquée par la pandémie de COVID-19 et reconstruire en mieux, il faudra continuer à adopter une approche mobilisant toutes les composantes des sociétés, l’ensemble des pouvoirs publics et le monde entier dans un esprit de compassion et de solidarité. Facteur essentiel d’une communication harmonieuse entre les peuples, le multilinguisme revêt plus que jamais une importance toute particulière pour l’ONU car il favorise la tolérance et assure la participation effective de tous

pages.description: The foresight of a primary school teacher in Wales helped to create one of the best attacking full-backs of the 1970s
pages.text: JPR Williams: a revolutionary, a fighter and the ultimate competitor | Wales rugby union team | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation JPR Williams: a rugby union great who changed full-back role – video obituary Wales rugby union team This article is more than 2 years old JPR Williams: a revolutionary, a fighter and the ultimate competitor This article is more than 2 years old Paul Rees The foresight of a primary school teacher in Wales helped to create one of the best attacking full-backs of the 1970s Tue 9 Jan 2024 12.28 EST Last modified on Wed 10 Jan 2024 05.27 EST Share J PR Williams described himself as a diehard Corinthian, but he was also a revolutionary. When he made his debut for Wales against Scotland in 1969, it was in a position then regarded as the last line of defence. Only 15 tries had been scored by full-backs in major Test matches in 88 years, but the former British junior tennis champion changed the dynamic and smoothed the way for players such as Andy Irvine, Serge Blanco and John Gallagher. Williams, who qualified as an orthopaedic surgeon while playing for London Welsh, scored six tries in his 55 internationals for Wales, five against England, an opponent he boasted a 100% success rate against in 11 Tests. He was qualified to wear the white jersey as his mother, Margaret, was born in Rochdale, but there was never the remotest chance of a boy born and raised in the Bridgend area turning his back on his homeland. But Guerrero still recognizes the importance of continuing his education despite having a front-row seat to the genome industry since its inception. Guerrero received a degree in biology from University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) in 1992, and joined the workforce of thousands of sequencers mapping DNA. However, six years after leaving his job as a sequencing associate at Incyte, a lecturer at UC Berkeley informed Guerrero that the technology used to sequence the human genome had already become obsolete. “This stark contrast highlights the rapid pace of technological evolution in this field,” says Guerrero. “Motivated by this insight, I decided to return to school, starting with a course in genetics.” That’s when Guerrero enrolled as a part-time student at Pasadena City College in Los Angeles in 2016. Since then, he continues to deepen his knowledge with MIT Open Learning educational resources. “I decided to update my skills in the sciences because they change rapidly,” says Guerrero. pages.text: Juan Mata: Former Spain midfielder retires aged 38 - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Mata celebrates winning Euro 2012 with Spain Published 18 November 2026 Former Spain midfielder Juan Mata has announced his retirement from playing at the age of 38. Mata, who made 41 international appearances, was part of the Spain squad that won the 2010 World Cup, and he helped his country win the European Championship two years later when he scored in the 4-0 final victory against Italy. A former Real Madrid youth player, he joined Valencia in 2007 before a move to Chelsea in August 2011 where he won the Champions League, Europa League and FA Cup. Mata moved to Manchester United in January 2014 and helped them claim the Europa League, FA Cup and League Cup prior to his departure in 2022. He went on to have spells at Turkish side Galatasaray and Vissel Kobe in Japan before he played for Australian sides Western Sydney Wanderers and Melbourne Victory. "Football will never leave my life," said Mata. "There are so many ways to continue loving the game, so many ways to keep using it as a vehicle for development. "I may stop playing professionally, but I will never stop being a footballer." Mata was Chelsea's player of the year in both full seasons he was at Stamford Bridge. He made 82 league appearances for the club, scoring 18 goals. "What a player," Chelsea posted on social media. This weekend, I was at State of the Map 2026, the international OpenStreetMap conference, which took place in Paris this year. Here’s a brief, personal feedback and a round-up of a few presentations that stood out for me. You can also find all the videos at https://peertube.openstreetmap.fr . NB: there is a French version here . This one was translated with the help of DeepL translate. The most inspiring: cartes.app Inspiring: cartes.app is a slightly mad project aimed at creating a new Google Maps, but without its car-centric bias. It started with a single contributor, but he’s managed to build a strong team around him: he has the insight to use the best open-source software components for his project – MapLibre for map navigation, vector tiles for map rendering, Photon for geocoding, and Transitious for public transport. Today, the developer is no longer working alone: he is securing funding and attracting contributors from around the world to improve his app and translate it so it can reach a global audience. It’s a wonderful project worth supporting, and you can do so by subscribing to cartes.app premium for just €1 a month. More Information The clocks developed by Ye and his colleagues are so precise that they would neither gain nor lose one second in 15 billion years, roughly the age of the universe. Determined to give Wacheke a shot, Odongo turned to MIT OpenCourseWare to create a six-month “bridging course” modeled after the classes she once took as a computer science student. Part of MIT Open Learning, OpenCourseWare offers free, online, open educational resources from more than 2,500 courses that span the MIT undergraduate and graduate curriculum. “Wacheke had the potential and interest to do the work that needed to be done, so the way to solve this was for me to literally create a path for her to get that work done,” says Odongo, founder and CEO of Senga Technologies. Developers, Odongo says, are not easy to find. The grooves are deep and warmly familiar, with wistful reflections on love and longing. But even in the brightest moments, there's often a thread of mystery and melancholy that leaves you questioning whether everything is as it seems. Fronted by the trio of Tom McFarland, Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto, Jungle is known for fluid live sets, with songs that spill into each other. True to form, at the Tiny Desk, they perform more than a half-dozen tracks that run together in a single, continuous groove. pages.text: Jurassic period information and facts | National Geographic SCIENCE What is the Jurassic period and why did it end? The heyday of dinosaurs, the Jurassic era saw Earth’s climate change from hot and dry to humid and subtropical. The Jurassic period was characterized by a warm, wet climate that gave rise to lush vegetation and abundant life. Many new dinosaurs emerged—in great numbers. Above, Dimorphodon reptiles fly over a herd of Mamenchisaurus dinosaurs coming down to a river for a drink. Illustration by CoreyFord, Getty Images By National Geographic Staff Last updated August 18, 2025 The Jurassic is a geologic period that took place about 201.3 million years to 145 million years ago and constitutes the middle part of the Mesozoic era . The Jurassic period was named after the Jura limestone deposits in the Jura Mountains, discovered by German geologist Alexander von Humboldt . Building on this find, French scientist Alexandre Brongniart later coined the Jurassic period. There are three Jurassic time periods: early, middle, and late. Overall, the Jurassic gives us a particularly well-preserved fossil record of prehistoric life, which included theropod dinosaurs that scientists believe evolved to become birds . Thanks to this rich record, we know that the Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs roaming a tropical Earth filled with ferns, flowering plants, and conifers. It was also a time when sea monsters, sharks, and blood-red plankton filled inland seas borne of crumbling landmasses. Here’s what the Jurassic period was really like. pages.text: Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Skip Navigation Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) May 01, 2024 The Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) is a Census Bureau experimental data product that measures the economic and health outcomes of people who have been involved with the criminal justice system. Criminal justice involvement can include criminal charges, prison releases, and probation and parole sentences. Outcomes measured include employment, earnings, government program participation, and mortality. JOE is a collaboration between the U.S. Census Bureau and the University of Michigan that uses Criminal Justice Administrative Records System (CJARS) data to better understand how people involved in the justice system reintegrate into society. JOE covers criminal justice system involvement at any point between 2000 and 2020. Actual coverage of justice involvement depends on the coverage of agencies in the CJARS data, while coverage of outcomes depends on the availability of source data at the Census Bureau. Data users can download JOE data below or interact directly with the JOE data using the data visualization tool hosted by the University of Michigan. The tool includes additional justice-related outcomes created from CJARS without Census Bureau data.
